summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive browser-based space survival simulation designed for young explorers ages 7 to 12. Players take on the role of mission lead at Shackleton Crater on the Moon or Jezero Crater on Mars, managing battery power, cabin air, hydroponic crops, crew fitness, and scientific rock analysis in real time while fellow crewmates rest.

To address the challenge of teaching real spaceflight hazards through engaging play, our game integrates live 30-day solar flare telemetry from NASA’s DONKI API alongside an offline archive of historic X-class solar storms, surface radiation measurements from Chang’e 4 and Curiosity RAD, and microgravity health research from NASA OSDR. When a solar particle storm approaches, players must keep their radio dish powered to hear warnings and sprint into a thick-walled regolith storm cellar that cuts storm radiation by 90%.

By turning abstract physics—like millisieverts, cosmic rays, and power budgets—into hands-on cause-and-effect decisions, the project inspires the Artemis generation and makes real space agency data accessible in any classroom or home browser.
details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Team: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer (Ebaad, Shayan, Ali)

Target Audience: Young Explorers (Ages 7–12) & Educators

1. What It Does & How It Works

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive browser-based survival and resource-management simulation that places players in the boots of a mission lead at either Shackleton Crater on the Moon or Jezero Crater on Mars. While fellow crewmates Amira and Leo rest after landing, the player walks around the outpost—clicking to move or using keyboard controls—to manage life support, scientific discovery, and solar storm safety in real time.

  • Dual-Scene Gameplay (EVA & Habitat): Outside on the planetary surface, players wipe lunar or Martian dust off solar panels, reset tripped breakers, and collect glowing rock samples before their Suit Air runs out. Inside the pressurized dome, players analyze rocks in the Science Lab, plant and harvest crops under Grow Lights, ride the Exercise Bike to prevent muscle and bone loss, maintain the Air Scrubber filter, and toggle the Radio Dish to receive Earth warnings.
  • Real-Time Power & Life-Support Trade-Offs: Solar panels only generate electricity during daylight hours, while the scrubber, grow lights, radio, and lab continuously drain the battery. Players must make strategic decisions—such as turning off the grow lights or radio at night—to avoid a blackout.
  • Real NASA Space Weather Integration: The simulation connects directly to NASA’s DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) API (with a built-in curated archive of historic X-class solar flares and coronal mass ejections for instant offline play). When a solar particle storm approaches, an active radio dish triggers an early warning siren, prompting the player to sprint into the thick-walled Regolith Storm Cellar, which cuts solar storm radiation by 90%.
  • Shareable Mission Seeds & Telemetry Debrief: Every mission generates a deterministic Mission Code (e.g., MM-9339) so classmates or friends can face the exact same storms and rock sites. Afterward, a Mission Debrief awards 1 to 3 stars, charts day-by-day telemetry curves (Air, Battery, Food, and Radiation against solar storm bands), and explains the real NASA science behind every outcome.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Turns Abstract Space Physics into Intuition: Concepts like millisieverts (mSv), galactic cosmic rays (GCRs), coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and regolith shielding are hard for 7-to-12-year-olds to grasp from a textbook. By feeling the urgency of a storm siren or watching battery levels drop when panels get dusty, kids build an intuitive, cause-and-effect understanding of space survival.
  • Bridges Classroom Science with Live Space Agency Data: By connecting a free NASA API key—or playing Today’s Mission, which gives every player worldwide the same daily seed—students experience real solar activity recorded by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory and space weather monitors.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Because the entire game runs smoothly in any modern desktop or mobile browser without installations, logins, or heavy hardware requirements, it is immediately usable in classrooms, libraries, and homes worldwide.
  • Intended Impact: To spark curiosity in STEM and human spaceflight among the Artemis generation, empowering young learners to think like mission controllers and planetary scientists while appreciating the real engineering challenges of living on the Moon and Mars.

3. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Coding Languages: Vanilla HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+)—built with zero external runtime frameworks or game-engine dependencies for instant loading and maximum compatibility.
    • Custom HTML5 2D Canvas renderer featuring procedural planetary terrain generation (craters, regolith, footprints), dynamic day/night sun-angle shadows, particle systems, and a 10.5-second animated launch-and-landing cinematic.
    • Synthesized Web Audio API sound engine generating procedural footsteps, airlock hisses, radio blips, and storm sirens without external audio file overhead.
    • NASA DONKI API (FLR solar flare and SEP solar energetic particle endpoints) plus an embedded archive of verified historic solar storms (e.g., the September 2017 AR 2673 X-class events).
    • Chang’e 4 & Mars Curiosity RAD surface radiation datasets (1.37 mSv/day on the Moon vs. 0.64 mSv/day on Mars).
    • NASA JPL (September 2017 Mars surface radiation spike data) and NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR Study OSD-342) (microgravity muscle and bone loss research).
    • Headless Node.js Simulation Balance Bot (balance-bot.js) engineered to run automated playthroughs across all worlds and difficulty tiers (Easy / Cadet, Medium / Pilot, Hard / Commander) to verify fairness, resource pacing, and winnability.
    • Git & GitHub for version control and static web hosting, alongside standard consumer laptops and mobile devices for cross-screen playtesting.

4. How Our Project Is Creative

  • Real Radiation Physics Translated into Level Design: Rather than treating radiation as an arbitrary "poison bar," we separated everyday galactic cosmic rays (which thick walls only reduce by 10–20%) from solar storm particles (which the Regolith Storm Cellar cuts by 90%). This teaches kids why real lunar and Martian habitats use regolith sandbags and water walls for storm shelters.
  • Planetary Realism Built into Gameplay Mechanics: Choosing Mars isn't just a palette swap—Mars features lower gravity hops, weaker sunlight on solar panels, regional dust storms, and communication delays that shorten storm warning lead times compared to the Moon's 1.3-second radio delay.
  • Decoupled Simulation & Headless Balance Bot: Separating the pure simulation core from the canvas renderer allowed us to build an AI playtester that runs dozens of simulated 5-to-9-day missions in milliseconds, ensuring the game is challenging yet always fair.

5. Factors Our Team Considered

  • Age-Appropriate Readability & Cognitive Load (Ages 7–12):
    • Used Atkinson Hyperlegible and Chakra Petch typography for clear letterforms and high-contrast numbers.
    • Designed an adaptive Mission Control Hint System that guides first-time players step-by-step on Easy (Cadet) mode (or whenever toggled on) without overwhelming experienced players.
    • Paired distinct icons, color coding, and text labels on every meter so information never relies on color alone.
    • Respected prefers-reduced-motion system settings to disable screen shake, flashing borders, and heavy particle streaks for motion-sensitive players.
    • Supported both tap/click-to-walk (ideal for tablets and Chromebooks) and WASD / Arrow + E keyboard controls.
    • Because school networks or public demos may block external APIs or rate-limit requests, the game gracefully falls back to its built-in archive of real NASA storms whenever offline or without an API key—and stores optional user API keys strictly in local browser storage.
